summary.title: Why the same workout stops working
points: The body adapts to a repeated demand; once adapted, the same session only maintains.
Progressive overload: make the demand grow with weight, reps, sets, tempo or a harder version.
The biggest benefit comes from going from no strength training to some (ACSM 2026).
You need a plan that gets a little harder each week, and that you'll follow.

exercises.scenario: For six months you've done 3 × 12 goblet squats with the same 12 kg kettlebell.

questions.prompt: What's most likely happening?
options: You're mostly maintaining
You're overtraining because you squat every single week
You're still progressing at the rate you did in month one, just more slowly to notice
You're losing muscle because twelve reps is too many to build anything
questions.explanation: The demand stopped being new months ago.

questions.prompt: You have no heavier kettlebell. Which change still counts as overload?
options: Taking longer rests so each set feels easier
Switching music during the session to stay motivated
Doing the same sets on a different day of the week
Adding reps, or slowing the lowering phase
questions.explanation: Reps and tempo are overload; Module 6 covers the rest.

exercises.scenario: A friend says 'there's no point lifting unless you follow a perfect programme'.

questions.prompt: What does the 2026 ACSM position stand say?
options: Programmes only work if every set goes to failure
Beginners should wait until they can lift 80% of their 1RM
Any training beats none; the biggest jump is from none to some
Only a periodised programme designed by a coach produces gains
questions.explanation: Consistency beats perfection.

questions.prompt: Which plan best follows progressive overload?
options: One very hard session a month
Same exercises, with one more rep per set each week until the top of the range
Exactly the same sets, reps and weights every week
A completely different workout every session to keep the body guessing
questions.explanation: Small, regular increases in demand.

summary.title: Stress, recovery, adaptation
points: Right after training you're weaker; improvement happens during recovery.
Muscle building stays raised for about a day or two after a session.
Fitness–fatigue model: fitness builds slowly and lasts; fatigue builds fast and fades.
Performance on the day is roughly fitness minus fatigue.
Sleep, food and rest days are part of the programme.

exercises.scenario: You trained hard Monday and Wednesday and feel flat on Thursday.

questions.prompt: What does the fitness–fatigue model suggest?
options: You should stop training for at least a month
Two sessions a week is always too much for anyone
You've lost fitness since Monday and need an extra session today
Fatigue is masking fitness you've built
questions.explanation: A lighter day usually reveals the fitness underneath.

questions.prompt: With 2–3 full-body sessions a week, what spacing fits best?
options: Three days in a row, then four days off to recover fully
Two sessions on the same day, morning and evening
At least one day between sessions
Any spacing, since recovery doesn't matter for strength
questions.explanation: It gives muscle building time to run its course.

exercises.scenario: A colleague trains hard every day, sleeps 5 hours, and isn't improving.

questions.prompt: What's the most likely cause?
options: Too little recovery: fatigue keeps stacking
Not enough variety in the music
Too much rest between sessions, so fitness fades
Training too lightly to create any stimulus at all
questions.explanation: Adaptation happens during recovery.

questions.prompt: When is the supercompensation curve misleading?
options: Only when the session is cardio rather than weights
When taken literally: it's a simplified picture
Never: it's an exact model of how each muscle recovers
Only for people over 60, whose recovery is different
questions.explanation: The fitness–fatigue model is the better description.

summary.title: You get what you train
points: Specificity: the body adapts to the type of demand you give it.
Running, cycling and racket sports build the aerobic engine, not maximal strength.
Muscle and strength need resistance training: a load against your muscles.
Strength also carries over to sprinting, jumping and court sports.

exercises.scenario: You run and play football, and want more upper-body muscle.

questions.prompt: What's the most direct route?
options: Stretching the chest and shoulders before every game
More football matches each week
Upper-body resistance training
Longer and faster runs, to burn more fat and reveal the muscle underneath
questions.explanation: Upper-body muscle grows from upper-body loading.

questions.prompt: Which counts as resistance training?
options: A long yoga stretch held for two minutes
Push-ups, kettlebell rows, band presses
A 10 km run at a steady pace
Only exercises done on gym machines with weight stacks
questions.explanation: Any load counts: weights, bands, bodyweight.

exercises.scenario: A tennis player asks whether squats will make them slower.

questions.prompt: What's the better answer?
options: Stronger legs and hips usually help sprints and changes of direction
Only if they squat on the same day as every match
Yes: strength training always reduces speed in racket sports
Squats only help long-distance runners
questions.explanation: Strength carries over; specificity guides the choice.

questions.prompt: Which result matches 'heavy lifts, about 1–6 reps'?
options: Power from light, fast lifts
Mobility
Aerobic endurance for long matches
Maximal strength
questions.explanation: Each kind of training has a main result.

summary.title: A quick health check
points: Strength training is safe for most healthy adults who start at a sensible level.
Fill in the PAR-Q+: all 'no' means start gradually; any 'yes' leads to follow-up questions.
It asks about heart conditions, chest pain, dizziness, chronic conditions, medicines, bones and joints.
Stop for chest pain or pressure, dizziness, unusual breathlessness or palpitations.
Muscle burn and next-day soreness are normal; sharp or joint pain isn't.

exercises.scenario: Mid-session, you feel chest pressure and dizziness.

questions.prompt: What do you do?
options: Slow down, finish the set, then rest a little longer
Stop and seek medical advice
Switch to stretching for the rest of the session
Drink water and continue with a lighter kettlebell
questions.explanation: These are stop signs, not normal discomfort.

questions.prompt: You answer 'yes' to one PAR-Q+ general question. What's next?
options: The follow-up questions, which may point to a professional
Do the baseline tests to see if it matters
Nothing: one 'yes' is fine for everybody
Stop all exercise permanently
questions.explanation: The follow-ups decide whether to go ahead.

exercises.scenario: The day after your first session your legs ache when you walk down stairs.

questions.prompt: How should you read that?
options: A sign of injury that needs a doctor before training again
A PAR-Q+ 'yes' answer
Proof the session was too light
Normal next-day muscle soreness
questions.explanation: Soreness is expected; sharp or joint pain isn't.

questions.prompt: When should you redo the PAR-Q+?
options: Every week before training
Only once in your life, before your very first session
Whenever your health changes
Only after a new personal best
questions.explanation: It's updated yearly too.

summary.title: Baseline tests
points: A baseline is a set of measures taken before you start and repeated every 4–12 weeks.
Strength and core: push-ups, goblet squat at 12 kg (stop ~2 short, cap 30), front and side planks.
Engine: resting heart rate on waking, and a 3-minute step test.
Body: waist midway between lowest rib and hip bone, plus photos.
Compare only with yourself; keep the same order and time of day.

questions.prompt: What keeps the result comparable?
options: A new set of tests that better matches what you trained recently
Testing straight after a hard football match
Same tests, order, warm-up and time of day
Comparing your numbers with online norm tables
questions.explanation: Consistency makes the comparison mean something.

questions.prompt: Your step-test heart rate drops from 120 to 108. What does it suggest?
options: Better aerobic fitness
Less fitness, because a lower number is worse
A fault in the test, since heart rate never changes with training
Dehydration
questions.explanation: Lower recovery heart rate is fitter.

exercises.scenario: Your weight is unchanged after 8 weeks.

questions.prompt: Which baseline measures matter most now?
options: Resting heart rate only
Waist, photos and strength results
Only body weight, since it's the most precise measure available at home
None; the programme has failed
questions.explanation: Weight alone can hide recomposition (Module 1).

questions.prompt: Where do you measure your waist?
options: At the widest point of the hips, wherever the belt sits that day
At the navel after a deep breath in
Just under the chest
Midway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone
questions.explanation: WHO STEPS protocol, at the end of a normal breath out.

summary.title: How the body adapts
points: The body adapts to a repeated demand, so the demand has to grow.
Improvement happens during recovery; fatigue can hide fitness for a few days.
You get what you train: cardio builds the engine, not much muscle or strength.
Resistance training with weights, bands or bodyweight covers muscle and strength.
Small weekly increases beat a perfect plan you don't follow.

exercises.scenario: Your routine for a year: running twice a week and the same 20-minute dumbbell circuit with 6 kg.

questions.prompt: Why have results stalled?
options: Twice a week is too much cardio for anyone
Dumbbells under 10 kg can't build anything at all
Running cancels out all the effects of the dumbbell circuit
The body has adapted and the demand never grew
questions.explanation: Same demand, same result: maintenance.

questions.prompt: What's the first change you'd make?
options: Make the circuit progressively harder each week
Stop running entirely to protect muscle
Add a third run so the body has a new stimulus
Change every exercise every session
questions.explanation: Overload is what's missing.

questions.prompt: Explain in two sentences why rest days help you get stronger.
questions.modelAnswer: A session creates fatigue and a signal to adapt; the repair and rebuilding happen afterwards, during recovery. Without enough rest, sleep and food, fatigue piles up and the adaptation doesn't show.

exercises.scenario: A friend says 'cardio is all I need, it works the whole body'.

questions.prompt: What does specificity say?
options: Cardio builds every quality equally if you do enough of it
Specificity only applies to professional athletes
Cardio builds endurance, not maximal strength or much upper-body muscle
Cardio builds strength but not endurance
questions.explanation: You get what you train.

questions.prompt: Which model explains feeling stronger after an easy week?
options: The PAR-Q+ screening flow
The fitness–fatigue model
The specificity principle
The energy balance equation
questions.explanation: Fatigue fades fast; fitness remains.

summary.title: Starting safely and measuring
points: Screen yourself with the PAR-Q+, and know the stop signs.
Take baseline tests: push-ups, goblet squat, planks, heart rate, step test, waist, photos.
Re-test every 4–12 weeks in the same way.
The training loop: plan, do, log, adjust.
Without a log there's nothing to adjust from.

exercises.scenario: You're about to start the course programme next Monday.

questions.prompt: What do you do this week?
options: PAR-Q+, then baseline tests, then a goal card
Buy all the equipment first, then decide what to test later
Start with the hardest session to see where you stand
Skip testing, since the scale is enough
questions.explanation: Screen, measure, then plan.

questions.prompt: Which step of the loop is most often missing?
options: The warm-up before every session
Log and adjust
Doing the session itself
Buying new kit each month
questions.explanation: No log, no adjustment, no progress.

questions.prompt: List the six baseline tests in one line.
questions.modelAnswer: Push-ups, goblet squat at 12 kg, front plank, side plank (each side), resting heart rate with a step test, and waist with photos.

exercises.scenario: After 4 weeks: push-ups 15 → 19, waist −1 cm, weight unchanged.

questions.prompt: What do you conclude?
options: Nothing has changed, because the scale didn't move at all
Stop and restart with a different programme
It's working; keep the loop going
The tests were done wrong
questions.explanation: Strength and waist moved; weight can lag.

questions.prompt: When do you re-test next?
options: Only at the end of the year
Only when you feel stronger
Every day, to track every small change
In another 4–12 weeks, same protocol
questions.explanation: Regular, consistent checks.

summary.title: How training works: the whole picture
points: The body adapts, so the demand must keep growing: progressive overload.
Gains happen during recovery; fatigue can mask fitness for days.
You get what you train: muscle and strength need resistance training.
Screen with the PAR-Q+ and know the stop signs.
Measure a baseline and run the loop: plan, do, log, adjust.

exercises.scenario: You're coaching a friend who runs 3 times a week and wants to 'tone up'.

questions.prompt: What do you add first?
options: A new random workout every day from social media
Two full-body resistance sessions with a progression plan
A fourth weekly run at a faster pace, to burn more calories
Daily stretching instead of strength work
questions.explanation: Specificity plus overload.

questions.prompt: How will you know it's working?
options: Check the scale every morning and react to each change
Ask whether the sessions feel hard
Count the calories burned on a watch
Re-test the baseline after 4–12 weeks
questions.explanation: Compare with their own starting point.

questions.prompt: They feel tired and weak after three hard days in a row. What's your call?
options: An easier day: fatigue is masking fitness
Stop training for a month
Switch to only cardio
Push harder to break through
questions.explanation: Recovery reveals the fitness.

exercises.scenario: Your own routine: same weights, same reps, mostly cardio.

questions.prompt: Which two principles does it ignore?
options: Energy balance and protein
Recovery and screening
Progressive overload and specificity
Mobility and flexibility
questions.explanation: No growing demand, and no strength-specific training.

questions.prompt: What does 'any training beats none' mean for a busy week?
options: Skip the week entirely unless you can do the full plan
Double the next week to make up for it
Only long sessions produce adaptation
A short session still counts; keep the habit
questions.explanation: Consistency matters most.

questions.prompt: Describe the training loop and say which step you'll start doing differently.
questions.modelAnswer: Plan the week, do the sessions while making one thing harder, log what you did and how hard it felt, then adjust next week's targets from the log. Most people start by adding the log, because without it nothing gets adjusted.
